title: The rabbit: rolling, hopping and bolting
summary: The rabbit target: how it rolls, hops and bolts, why it often needs less lead than you expect, and the No Bird rule when it breaks by itself.

body.html: A rabbit is a 110 mm target with a thick, strong rim, thrown on its edge so that it rolls along the ground like a running hare. It is a special target, so in Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ it must be shown on the target menu of the stand.
The rabbit rolls and bounces along the ground; watch how low it stays and how it hops.
body.heading: Watch how the target flies

body.html: Coaches describe how it runs: a rolling rabbit runs smoothly; a hopping (bouncing) rabbit jumps on bumps and stones; a bolting rabbit bursts out of cover and runs fast. Rabbits can go across, towards or away from the shooter.

A rabbit is heavy and slows down quickly, so shooters often shoot too far in front of it (over-lead). Many coaches suggest keeping the gun low and shooting at the bottom front edge of the rabbit. Then, if it suddenly hops, it jumps up into the shot rather than over it. Often it is visible only in a short gap between bushes, so the break point needs careful planning.

Rules: each target, the rabbit included, is shot with the gun at the shoulder; shooting from the hip is not allowed in either discipline. A special case: you miss with the first shot, and before you can fire the second the rabbit breaks by itself, for example on a stone. That is a No Bird, and the rabbit is thrown again. On the repeat only a hit with the second shot counts, so you fire the first shot deliberately wide. If you break it with the first shot, it is scored as a miss (zero).

Safety matters especially with rabbits, because they run low near the ground. Shoot only inside the permitted zone, never swing the barrels towards people or traps, and do not shoot beyond a shooting limit.
“Fur and feather” is English Sporting slang for a pair of a rabbit (“fur”) and an aerial target (“feather”).

notes.html: Shooters' names for the rabbit differ between languages. Choose one word and keep it all session.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: It hops on that bump — stay under it and keep moving.
phrases.meaning: The rabbit jumps at a known spot; keep the gun low and moving.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Put the shot on the bottom edge of the rabbit, not over it.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: It slows down a lot — less lead than you think.
phrases.meaning: The rabbit loses speed quickly, so it needs a smaller lead.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Fur and feather: rabbit first, before it reaches the bushes.
phrases.meaning: In the rabbit-plus-bird pair, shoot the rabbit first because it disappears into cover.

key_points.html: Rabbit: 110 mm, thick rim, rolls on its edge along the ground.
Rolling, hopping (bouncing), bolting: describe how it runs.
It slows quickly: do not shoot too far in front; keep the gun low.
Always shot from the shoulder; a rabbit that breaks by itself after a first-shot miss is a No Bird.
“Fur and feather” = rabbit + aerial target pair.

quiz.q: The first shot misses a rabbit, then it breaks on a stone before the second shot. What happens?

options.text: It is scored as a hit, since it broke
It is scored zero for the first miss
No Bird: repeated, only a second-shot break counts
The shooter just moves to the next target

quiz.explain: Both rulebooks treat this as a No Bird; on the repeat the shooter must deliberately miss with the first shot.

quiz.q: Why do coaches warn against too much lead on a rabbit?

options.text: It is heavy and slows quickly
It is smaller than a mini

quiz.explain: A rabbit has a thick rim and rolls on the ground, losing speed fast. So the lead you would give a flying crosser sends the shot ahead of the rabbit: a miss in front.

options.text: A pair of a rabbit and an aerial target
A target with feathers glued on

quiz.explain: In English Sporting slang “fur” is the rabbit and “feather” the flying target.
